title: Are we in a simulation?
dek: A count in sixties, written down more than four thousand years ago, still divides the hour and the circle. Related numbers also show up in the sky. Two readings stay open.
socialHook: Sixty still divides the hour, the minute, and the circle. The numbers 72, 432, and 25,920 also meet in the sky. Both readings stay open.
socialTitle: Are the old counts a clock we kept, or a mark?
heroAlt: A diagram of a circle marked with many small ticks and one cobalt arc, beside a clay tablet. It shows a sixty-based count without printed numerals.

marginNote.label: Two readings stay open.
marginNote.body: The counts can be a tool people kept because it worked. They can also be read as a mark. The essay does not choose.

blocks.text: More than four thousand years ago, a scribe in Mesopotamia pressed a reed into wet clay and counted in sixties. The same count still divides the hour on a phone into sixty minutes, and each minute into sixty seconds.

A circle is also divided into 360 degrees, which is 6 times 60. The old numbers show up again in the slow wobble of Earth's axis, in figures given for the Sun, and in the speed of light. The numbers in this essay are 72, 432, and 25,920.

The question is whether a built world would leave a few numbers that keep meeting. Are we in a simulation? The question is not a joke, and it is not a verdict. Both readings stay on the table while you look at the counts.
Counting to sixty on one hand
Mesopotamian mathematics used base 60, not base 10. Sixty divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, and 30, so it is practical for dividing grain, land, silver, or the sky.

You can still find sixty on your own hand. Touch your thumb to each finger-bone in turn: three bones on each of four fingers makes twelve. Let the other hand keep count of the rounds, one finger at a time, up to five. Twelve times five is sixty. No abacus, no clay, just a body.

blocks.alt: A photograph of a hand counting to twelve by touching the finger-bones with the thumb.
blocks.caption: Photo: Rhetos / Wikimedia Commons, Mathe-AC Lernwerkstatt, Aachen, 2021. CC0.

blocks.text: There are two plain readings. A useful count may be a tool that worked, so people kept it. Or it may be surprising that the same count still runs the clock, the compass, and the circle thousands of years later. Both sentences can be true. The essay does not drop either one.
The slow wobble of the sky

Earth spins once a day and circles the Sun once a year. The axis also traces a slow circle against the stars. Astronomers call the motion the precession of the equinoxes. The pole star of the pyramid builders was not the pole star used now, because the axis has moved.

One full wobble takes roughly twenty-six thousand years, and a round figure long used for it is 25,920. Divide that by the 360 degrees of a circle and you get 72: one degree of sky about every 72 years, which is about one human lifetime. Divide 25,920 by 12, 24, 36, 48, and 60. The results are 2,160, 1,080, 720, 540, and 432.

blocks.alt: A 1902 printed diagram of the precession of the equinoxes, showing the slow wobble of Earth's axis.
blocks.caption: Image: Public Domain / Simon Newcomb, Astronomy for Everybody, 1902.

blocks.text: The number 432 also appears in other familiar figures. A day has 86,400 seconds. The Sun's diameter is often given as about 864,000 miles. The Moon's diameter is about 2,160 miles, the same as 25,920 divided by 12. And 432 multiplied by itself is 186,624, which sits close to the speed of light in miles per second.

Miles and seconds are units people chose. If you swap the units, some of these matches drift apart. The unit choice belongs in the comparison. So does a second fact. The numbers 12, 60, 72, 360, and 25,920 already met one another before anyone invented a mile. They show up in a hand count, a clock, a circle, and the slow turn of the sky.
Sumer, pine cones, and standing waves

Sumer appears in the record with writing, wheels, boats, looms, ploughs, and organised mathematics, all in a short stretch of time. The Sumerian King List opens by saying that kingship was lowered from heaven. Later Mesopotamian reliefs show winged figures carrying a small bucket and a cone. The reliefs do not say what the figures are doing.

One reading is that the stories remember teachers, and that knowledge was handed down rather than only invented. Another reading is that cities have always explained power by saying it came from above. The texts record both kinds of sentence. They do not force one reading.

A pine cone is part of the same discussion. Its seed scales often spiral in counts that follow the Fibonacci sequence. The pineal gland sits deep in the brain, and its shape has reminded people of a small pine cone. Some writers then say the gland might receive a signal, and that a tone might be one of those signals. The shape is a resemblance. It is not a test of that claim.

blocks.alt: A pine cone photographed from above, its scales spiralling out from the centre.
blocks.caption: Photo: Richard Flink / Wikimedia Commons, 2008. CC BY-SA 2.0.

blocks.text: The tones named in this conversation are 144, 288, 360, and 432. Sound can also arrange matter. If you scatter sand on a metal plate and draw a bow along the edge, the grains move into a geometric figure along the lines where the plate stays still. The demonstration is called cymatics, and it is ordinary physics. Whether 432 hertz is special, or one pitch among many that can draw a figure, is not settled by the plate.

blocks.alt: A square metal plate with sand gathered into a symmetrical standing-wave pattern.
blocks.caption: Photo: High Contrast / Wikimedia Commons, 2011. CC BY 3.0 DE.

blocks.text: Two readings of the same counts

People tend to sort these numbers in three ways. One reading says a built world would reuse a few ratios on purpose. A second reading says people are good at finding patterns. A third reading says the meetings are coincidence and then stops. The third reading ends the comparison before it starts. Set it aside, and the first two readings can be compared.

The first reading says a built world could leave a few reused ratios, a clock that still matches the sky, a body count that matches a plant count, and stories that say the knowledge was handed down. A built world, on this reading, would not leave a signature. It would leave the same ratios in more than one place.

The second reading says people are good at finding patterns. The same skill that found the seasons can also join a hand count, a hymn, and a mile into one sentence. Some of those joins depend on units people invented. Some of them do not.

Either reading can be held without dropping the other. The counts are real. The slow circle of the axis is real. The sand on the plate really moves. What the repetition means is still a choice. Keeping both readings open is not a failure of the essay.
The numbers are in the sky and in the clock. What they mean is still open.
The same count can be a clock people kept because it worked, and it can be read as a mark someone left. The essay does not decide which reading is the whole story.
